parsed_answer.content:
When designing high-performance data structures in Java, the `HashMap` remains the cornerstone of key-value lookup operations. A fundamental design pattern baked into `java.util.HashMap` is the strict enforcement of power-of-2 capacities. Understanding why this constraint is recommended requires diving deep into the hashing mechanics, bitwise arithmetic, and collision resolution strategies used during bucket index computation. When a key is inserted, the `HashMap` invokes the `hashCode()` method, which is then subjected to a secondary perturbation function (the spread function: `h ^ (h >>> 16)`) to mitigate poor user-defined hash functions. The resulting integer hash code must then be mapped to an array index corresponding to the current table capacity.

The core reason powers of 2 are enforced lies in how index derivation is calculated. In a theoretical HashMap where capacity is an arbitrary prime or odd number, calculating the bucket index requires the modulo operator (`hash % capacity`). In modern CPU architectures, the integer division instruction required for modulo arithmetic is notoriously expensive, taking dozens of clock cycles. By enforcing that the capacity ($N$) is strictly a power of two ($2^k$), Java can replace the costly modulo operation with a lightning-fast bitwise AND operation: `hash & (N - 1)`. Because a power of 2 minus one results in a bitmask of consecutive ones in binary (e.g., $16 - 1 = 15$, which is `00001111` in binary), the bitwise AND operation isolates the lower bits instantly in a single CPU cycle, optimizing memory access paths.

rows: Requires perturbation to avoid lower-bit collisions
Distributes hashes evenly without bitmask correlation
Doubling capacity keeps existing bits stable
Requires full re-indexing and modulo recalculation

items: Bitmask Collisions and Lower-Bit Dependence: Without the perturbation function (`h >>> 16`), a power-of-2 capacity of size $16$ (`00001111`) would completely ignore the upper 16 bits of a 32-bit integer hash code during the `hash & (N - 1)` operation. If keys only differ in their upper bits, they would all map to index 0, causing catastrophic clustering.

The Resize and Rehash Optimization: When a HashMap reaches its threshold (Capacity * Load Factor), it doubles its capacity to maintain $O(1)$ amortized lookups. Because the new capacity is also a power of 2, the bitmask simply extends by one bit to the left. During resizing, an element's index either remains exactly the same or moves to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`, avoiding complex recalculations.

Automatic Capacity Rounding: Even if a developer instantiates a HashMap with a non-power-of-2 initial capacity (e.g., `new HashMap<>(10)`), the internal constructor uses a bit-twiddling algorithm (`tableSizeFor`) to find the smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to the requested argument (rounding 10 up to 16).

parsed_answer.content: Production Gotcha: Always initialize your HashMaps with an expected capacity if you know the data size beforehand, keeping in mind that it will be rounded up to the next power of 2. For instance, if you insert 1000 items with a default load factor of 0.75, the map needs a capacity of at least 1334. If you instantiate it with the default capacity (16), it will unnecessarily trigger multiple expensive array resize and rehash operations as it grows through 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1024.

title: Why is it recommended to use a power of 2 for HashMap capacity?
